deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Arbitrary Relocation

For restaurant operators, a relocation clause is not merely a logistical inconvenience; it is a potential death knell for the business. Landlords frequently insert relocation or reconfiguration provisions that grant them the unilateral right to move your premises to another unit within the development. The primary danger lies in the lack of specificity regarding what constitutes a comparable space. Without rigorous definitions, a landlord can move a high-visibility corner restaurant to a dead-end corridor, effectively destroying your foot traffic and brand equity.

Beyond mere visibility, the technical requirements of a restaurant lease make relocation uniquely expensive. Unlike a standard retail boutique, a restaurant relies on heavy-duty infrastructure, including grease traps, specialized HVAC, venting systems, and high-capacity plumbing. A landlord-driven move into a space lacking these utilities can trigger millions in unbudgeted capital expenditures. Furthermore, the loss of goodwill—the established customer base tied to a specific physical location—is often unrecoverable in a poorly executed move. If the new space lacks the necessary zoning or utility capacity, the tenant may find themselves legally bound to a space that cannot support their existing menu or volume.

Securing Your Operational Integrity

To mitigate these risks, your lease must move beyond simple comparability and establish strict, non-negotiable criteria for any relocation event. A sophisticated tenant must demand the following protections:

  • Infrastructure Parity: The new space must possess identical or superior utility capacities, specifically regarding venting, grease interceptors, and electrical loads.
  • Full Cost Indemnification: The landlord must bear 100% of all costs associated with the move, including demolition, construction, permitting, and professional fees.
  • Business Interruption Reimbursement: The clause must mandate compensation for lost revenue and increased labor costs during the transition period.
  • Visibility and Foot Traffic Guarantees: The new unit must be of equal or greater prominence, frontage, and accessibility.
  • Permitting and Licensing Continuity: The landlord must guarantee that the new space is legally zoned and capable of maintaining all existing health and liquor licenses.
